title: Chapter 12: Coffee With the Director
content: The wind on Ridge Road comes off the water and goes through Wren's jacket like it is looking for something it lost.

Kestrel House sits where the road turns, brick and white trim and a gravel drive raked into lines. She is eleven minutes early, so she stands at the gate for eleven minutes with the folder under her arm and watches the maples move.

Below the bluff the town is small enough to hold in one look. The Annex with its flat roof. The diner with its sign. The church with the bell that has been wrong since 1988. The river going through the middle of it like a seam, and nine houses on the east bank, and hers the last of them, with the boat shed and the landing and the place where the cable comes out of the water and climbs the hill to the wheel.
At nine exactly she rings the bell.
Celia Reeve opens the door in a cream sweater and no shoes. She looks at Wren's boots, and then at the folder, and something goes across her face and is put away.
"She is on the terrace," Celia says.
"Thank you."
"He is not here."
"I did not ask."
"Everybody asks." Celia steps back. "Go around the side. Do not go through the house. She does not like people going through the house."

The terrace is stone, with a low wall and a brass telescope on a tripod pointed north at the gate. Ottoline Reeve stands at the wall with a cup in her hand, grey linen, hair back, one ring. She does not turn around until Wren's boots are loud on the stone.
"Miss Aubrey. Sit."

There is a table with a silver pot, two cups, and a plate of figs cut in quarters. Ottoline pours without asking and sets the cup down with the handle turned out, and the coffee is better than anything served in Kestrel Bend, and Wren hates that she notices.

The terrace has a wool blanket folded over the back of an empty chair, a book face down with a ribbon in it, and a pair of pruning shears hung on the wall with the blades wiped clean. Everything up here is maintained. It is the most frightening room Wren has ever stood in.
"You walked up," Ottoline says.
"I do not have a car."
"You have a ferry."
"I had a ferry."

Ottoline looks at the gate. From up here it is a white shed on the water with the river coming out of the bottom of it, and a road along the top where the Authority's trucks go, and beyond it the lake the town is not allowed to see.

The telescope is pointed at the gate and not at the river. Wren checks without meaning to. The brass knob is worn bright on one side and the eyepiece is capped, and the cap has a film of dust on it, which means nobody has looked through this thing in weeks.
"Your grandfather ran nine hundred crossings a year," Ottoline says. "Give or take the ice. I looked it up."
"Then you know more than the county does."
"I know more than the county wants to." She sits. "I have read all forty-one of your filings. Every page. It took me two evenings."
"Did you enjoy them?"
"I did not." Ottoline lifts the pot and tops off her own cup. "You attached a page from a book to each one. A page with a name and a date in a hand that is not yours."
"Yes."
"Whose hand?"
"His. Then mine. Then his again."
Ottoline sets the pot down and takes an envelope from under the plate of figs.

"Ninety thousand dollars," she says. "It is a condolence settlement. It is not compensation. Compensation would be an admission and I am not authorized to admit anything, which you know, because you have read the statute."
Wren opens the envelope. The check is made out to Wren Aubrey, ninety thousand dollars and no cents, and it is signed in the same even hand that wrote her name on the envelope.
Under it are two pages, stapled once in the corner.
"Clause four," Ottoline says, "is the one you will object to."

Wren reads the whole thing, in order, the way she reads everything now. Nine clauses. Clause one is the payment. Clause two is confidentiality, with a schedule of exceptions that does not include the press. Clause three releases the Authority from all claims arising from the events of 12 September. Clause four states the cause.
Cause of loss: act of river.
"The deceased entered the water as a result of river conditions outside the control of any party," she reads aloud.
"Yes."
"He entered the water because the deck dropped six feet under him."
"The deck is the river."
"The deck is a boat. The river is what came over it."

Clause five says the Authority admits no liability, which is a sentence she has read forty times in the last three weeks and has stopped finding strange. Clause six is the one that makes her put the cup down.
"The claimant shall withdraw all filings made in connection with the above matter and shall not file further."
"That is standard," Ottoline says. "You cannot be paid and also be suing."
"It withdraws all of them. Not just mine."

"It withdraws yours. The others were never yours to file." Ottoline turns her cup a quarter turn on the saucer. "You filed them as a carrier. Nobody has ever asked me to rule on whether a carrier is a relationship. I would prefer not to."
"So this is the price of the forty-one."
"This is the price of you." Ottoline's eyes come up. "It is offered to the person whose grandfather is in the water. Not to the town. The town is not in the water."
Ottoline drinks her coffee. Somewhere below the bluff a truck goes along the gate road and the sound arrives a half second after the truck does.
"You are very close," she says. "You are one word away and you will not take it."
Wren turns the page. Schedule A is the payment. Schedule B is one line.
"Schedule B," she says. "The claimant shall deliver to the Authority the vessel's log, all volumes, for archival purposes."
"Yes."
"You want the book."

"I want the record whole." Ottoline leans back. "You have four hundred pages of the town in your kitchen and a photograph of every page on your telephone. I have a county with a hearing calendar and a river that does not care what either of us wants. If that book is lost, it is lost. If it is in the archive, it is not lost."
"It is not lost now. It is on the boat."
Ottoline looks at her a half second longer than the sentence deserves, and Wren understands that the Authority has been watching the house and not the landing.
"On a boat the county is preparing to condemn." Ottoline says it without pleasure. "I am not threatening you. I am telling you the arithmetic."
Wren puts the two pages flat on the table and takes the pen off the saucer, which is Ottoline's pen, a fountain pen with a nib that has been used enough to be somebody's.
"You said I was one word away," Wren says. "I will sign it if you change one thing."
"Name it."
"Clause four." She turns to page one and writes in the margin, in block letters, small: DROWNED. Then she writes the date, 4 Oct 2026, and her initials, W.A., and she puts the pen down.
Ottoline looks at the margin for a long time. The wind moves the edge of the page.
"You are asking me to admit a machine was wrong," she says.
"I am asking you to admit a man drowned."

"A man drowned. I have never said otherwise. I have said it to the county and I have said it in this house." Ottoline's voice does not rise. It does not need to. "What I cannot say is that the Authority drowned him. The Authority is not a person. The gate is not a person. The river is a machine with one moving part, and the part is silt, and everything I do up there is maintenance."
"Maintenance killed him."

"Silt kills him. Silt in the channel, silt in the intake, silt in the water the town drinks. If I do not move it, the intake blocks and this town has no water by August. That is not a theory. That happened in 1977 and the county has the photographs."
Wren picks up her cup and finds it empty and does not remember drinking it.
"There was no siren," she says.
Ottoline's hand stops on the pot.
"The siren is a courtesy," she says. "To the town."
"To the town," Wren says. "Not to the people on the water."
"The schedule is published. The schedule is the warning."
"The schedule said the twelfth."

Ottoline looks at her for a moment too long. Then she pours the last of the coffee into her own cup, and her hand is steady, and that is the only thing in the whole morning that Wren will remember as an answer.
"Someone will answer for the siren," Ottoline says. "Not the river. Someone."
Wren folds the two pages and puts them inside her jacket, and the check with them, and stands.
"That is my copy," Ottoline says.
"Then make another. You have a machine for it."
Ottoline almost smiles. It is not a warm thing. It is the way a person looks at a dog that has learned a trick faster than expected.
"Ninety thousand dollars is a real number, Miss Aubrey. It is a roof and a winter and a year of not counting fares. It will not be on this table in November."
"Nothing is on this table in November."
Wren is at the corner of the house, on the gravel, when Ottoline speaks again, without turning around.

"The condemnation is scheduled. The county will hear it and the ferry will go." A pause. "You will be given four minutes to speak. That is the whole of what I can do for you and it is more than the county wanted to give."
Wren stops.
"Four minutes."
"Four." Ottoline lifts her cup. "Spend them well."
Celia is standing at the corner of the house with both hands around a mug, and she has been there long enough to have heard the last part.
"Four minutes," Celia says.
"Four."

"My uncle drowned in ninety-eight and got a stone in nine days." She says it to the mug. Then her eyes come up and she is already stepping back toward the door. "Forget I said that. I have a thing in the oven."
She is gone before Wren can ask, and the door she goes through is the front door, which is the one she told Wren not to use.

Wren walks down the drive with the wind at her back and the folder empty under her arm. At the gate she stops and does the arithmetic, because arithmetic is what she has instead of a voice that carries.
Two hundred and forty seconds. At six seconds a name, she can read forty names into a microphone. She has four thousand.
She starts walking. She is already counting.
highlight: Coffee at Kestrel House, a settlement offer built on the words act of river, and Wren counting seconds per name.
